variant.text: The tasks are drawn from the clinical database MIMIC-IV version 2.2 (snapshot released in January 2023, hosted on PhysioNet), and every task record stores the identifier of its source patient record, so any task can be traced back to its origin.

To assess representativeness, we compared the age, sex and race distribution of the benchmark patients against the U.S. adult inpatient population reported in a national hospital discharge survey, and found differences of under five percentage points in every category.

The benchmark includes a safety test suite that measures unsafe outputs such as contraindicated medication orders, and a separate bias test that compares agent accuracy across patient demographic groups.

To limit contamination, the test split is held out and distributed only through gated access, and we measured verbatim overlap between the test tasks and a public web corpus, finding no exact matches.

The environment is frozen at release: the database snapshot, the software image and the simulated-patient language model are all pinned to fixed versions, and no external service is called at evaluation time other than the model under test.
To confirm that every task is solvable, we ran a scripted reference solution for each task through the grader; all 120 reference solutions were graded correct.
The grader checks both the intended state changes and that all other records remain unchanged, so out-of-scope modifications are detected and counted as failures.
Random-action agents achieve 3.1% success across tasks. Appendix tables document baseline success rates for each metric.
Across all 120 tasks, an agent with no actions scores 0.0%, while a random-action agent achieves 2.5%.
Every run applies temperature 0 with a fixed seed. The main text describes the policy of executing each task three times.
For each model, five independent runs per task employed separate random seeds at temperature 0.7. Reported scores represent the mean of these five independent runs.

To measure reliability, we ran each task eight times and report pass^8, the fraction of tasks solved in all eight runs, together with the agreement of the final environment state across the eight runs.
We evaluated GPT-4 and Claude as agents.

Each tool is defined by a JSON schema listing its name, arguments and argument types. The documentation states for every tool whether it only reads or also writes state, and describes what each tool returns, including the error message returned for invalid arguments. These tool descriptions are included in the agent prompt.

The write actions that change patient state (medication orders, notes and messages) are listed in a table. Writes are executed against a sandboxed copy of the record, and unnecessary or unsafe writes are penalised in the score. The agent prompt states that writes are sandboxed.
Grading operates on the final environment state. Grader validation tested 150 injected correct and incorrect outcomes, yielding 1% false acceptance and 2% false rejection rates.

Agents have no web access during runs and retrieval tools are restricted to the task environment, so answers cannot leak through external search. A private held-out split with hidden labels is kept off all public surfaces, and every released task carries a canary string.
